precedence: 1. Overrides recorded in this register (overrides[]). Each states its source; where an override corrects a project preset (OVR-03, OVR-04) it says so, and the override wins.
2. Explicit locks in the run's own preset block (project system_prompt: fao_editor1, fao_editor2, ...)
3. Live official databases the guide itself points to: NOCS export for country names (fao.org/nocs), FAO Term Portal for terminology
4. FAOSTYLE CB8081EN as captured in rules[] and fao_recommended_words.json
6. Oxford English Dictionary, first spelling listed

execution.notes: Patterns run on one paragraph at a time (DOCX paragraph or labelled-markdown line). Anchored patterns use (?m). The runner must enforce `scope` (body, heading, caption, table, footnote, reference ...) and mask quotations first (REF-12_3_3-006).
execution.input: DOCX run text is the reference input: it keeps non-breaking spaces, superscripts and italics. On markdown or plain text, rules whose check.requires includes 'nbsp' or 'formatting' are skipped and listed as not checked in the receipt.
execution.apply_policy: Calibration phase: every finding is reported as Verify, whatever its action. A rule is promoted to auto-apply only after it has run on at least three real manuscripts with no false positive; record that in calibration.status. Until then `action: Apply` means 'unambiguous once the editor has confirmed the hit'.

audit.note: Independent audit: fidelity sample 6/60 defects, regex noise, Appendix 2 pairing; all corrected.

overrides.guide_says: §7: redefinition advised where parts are likely to be read separately (chapters, front matter, boxes); not needed in annexes/appendices.
overrides.project_rule: Define at first mention in every chapter and self-standing section; boxes count as separate; annexes and appendices do not need redefinition.

overrides.guide_says: percent, never per cent; % only in figures and tables.
overrides.project_rule: Use percent in running text; normalize per cent and log once. % closed up in tables and figures.
overrides.source: fao_editor2 percent_in_text = word; conflicts.md §3 (the schema's client override permits but does not require per cent)

overrides.project_rule: Non-breaking space (U+00A0) in Word manuscripts; thin space only where a typesetting specification asks for it. This corrects the 001WRR preset (thousands_spacing = thin_space) for DOCX work; the override wins over the preset.
overrides.source: conflicts.md §4 (001WRR thousands_spacing = thin_space is overruled for DOCX)

overrides.guide_says: §5.6: spaced en dash for parenthetical asides; unspaced for ranges, relationships and equal-weight compounds.
overrides.project_rule: Resolve by function, as §5.6 does: spaced en dash for parenthetical asides and elaborations, unspaced for ranges, relationships and equal-weight compounds. This corrects fao_editor2 (dash_parenthetical_spacing = unspaced), which would otherwise close up parenthetical dashes against §5.6; the override wins over the preset. Em dashes are never correct.

overrides.guide_says: §4 spelling policy (-ize) with -yse verbs and listed -ise words (Appendix 2: advertise, comprise, liaise, merchandise, otherwise, ...).
overrides.project_rule: The project regex \b([A-Za-z]+?)ise\b -> \1ize is a candidate generator only, never auto-apply. Exceptions: the conflicts.md §6 list, every -ise word in Appendix 2 (header.ise_exceptions_from_appendix2), proper names with registered spelling, quotations.

overrides.guide_says: Not a FAOSTYLE rule; project pass.
overrides.project_rule: Use the 002ThV pass regex (27 verbs incl. modals), not the short schema validation regex.

overrides.guide_says: §3 writing guidance (keep sentences short); no numeric cap.

overrides.topic: Country names: live NOCS outranks the guide's printed examples
overrides.guide_says: §6.3.1: follow NOCS. Printed examples date from November 2024 (e.g. line 1180 'the Bahamas').
overrides.project_rule: The official NOCS export governs (e.g. 'The Bahamas' with capital T per NOCS since April 2025; 'the Gambia' lower case per NOCS; Naoero for Nauru from June 2026). Check with nocs_check.py.
overrides.source: FAOSTYLE §6.3.1 points to NOCS; NOCS export 30 October 2026. Note: fao_styleguide_schema.json and conflicts.md §10 give 'The Gambia', which NOCS does not support.

overrides.guide_says: §10.3: calendar ranges in full with en dash (2015–2025); crop and fiscal years with slash, compacted (2015/16).
overrides.project_rule: Follow the guide. The old schema's 2015–16 compacting (NUM-RANGE-004) is withdrawn.

overrides.guide_says: §10: one to ten in words, 11 upward in numerals.
overrides.project_rule: Follow the guide. The old schema's 'zero to nine' (NUM-WORDS-001) is withdrawn.

overrides.topic: Mandatory rules are never author choices
overrides.guide_says: FAOSTYLE applies to all FAO content.
overrides.project_rule: Where a rule of kind 'mandatory' has a fix the editor can make from the document and the guide (action Apply or Verify), the editor applies it and never offers the author a choice; an author reply does not override it. Rules with action Author are different: they ask the author for missing content (a source, a page number, a permission), not for a choice of form.
overrides.source: Project decision after the October 2026 NOCS slip (P4, P6)

overrides.guide_says: Implied: Appendix 2 closes up re- compounds (WRD entry for re- compounds), which gives reuse.
overrides.project_rule: reuse, without a hyphen; not re-use or re use.

rules.quote: The slash / should generally be avoided in running text.

rules.quote: Use non-breaking spaces to avoid number divisions at the end of lines.
rules.rule: Use non-breaking spaces (not ordinary spaces) as thousands separators.

check.notes: Pattern contains an ordinary space (U+0020) between digit groups; NBSP (U+00A0) and narrow NBSP (U+202F) pass. Run only on text extracted from DOCX with NBSPs preserved; the markdown conversion of the guide itself (and many labelled markdown exports) normalizes NBSP to ordinary spaces, so the guide's own examples (10 000) would match here and are therefore not listed as examples. Also applies to millions (line 1487).

rules.quote: It is acceptable to write 1000 through 9999 with no space where a space would look awkward (particularly in titles or headings) and when it is not specifically compared with another number in the thousands or higher, where the space would be required, e.g. between 5 000 and 10 000.
rules.rule: Numbers 1000-9999 may be written without a space, except when compared with another number in the thousands or higher, where the space is required.

check.notes: Flags an unspaced 4-digit number directly compared with a spaced number of 10 000 or more ("5000 and 10 000"). A 4-digit year next to a large number can be a false positive. Comparisons across a sentence need agent review. Whether the unspaced form is "awkward" is a judgement; the guide does not require consistency for 1000-9999 otherwise.

rules.quote_pdf: It is acceptable to write {+1000 }through {+9999 }with no space where a space would look awkward (particularly in titles or headings) and when it is not specifically compared with another number in the thousands or higher, where the space would be required, e.g. {+between }**{+5 000 }**{+and }**{+10 000}**.

rules.quote: Do not use spaces for years (e.g. 2007) or page numbers (e.g. p. 1402).
rules.rule: Do not use thousands spaces in years or page numbers.

check.notes: Flags "p. 1 402" and a spaced 4-digit year after a typical year preposition. A genuine quantity "of 2 000" can be a false positive; editor verifies.

rules.quote_pdf: Do not use spaces for years (e.g. {+2007}) or page numbers (e.g. {+p. 1402}).

rules.quote: For millions, use numerals separated by non-breaking spaces (e.g. 150 324 399) unless the last six numerals are zeros, in which case express these digits as million (e.g. 150 000 000 should be written as 150 million). The same principle holds for billions, trillions, etc.
rules.rule: Write millions (billions, trillions) as spaced numerals, but where the last six digits are zeros write the number with the word million (billion, trillion).

check.notes: Flags numbers ending in six zeros, spaced or unspaced. The guide itself writes "1 000 000 000" when defining the short scale (line 1492); definitional uses like that are false positives. Unclear whether the rule applies in tables.

rules.quote_pdf: For millions, use numerals separated by non-breaking spaces (e.g. {+150 324 399}) unless the last six numerals are zeros, in which case express these digits as {+million }(e.g. {-150 000 000 }should be written as {+150 }**{+million}**). The same principle holds for billions, trillions, etc.

rules.quote: Data are in general reported to three significant figures.
rules.rule: In general, report data to three significant figures.

check.notes: Judgement on data precision; the guide's own example 150 324 399 (line 1487) has nine significant figures, so apply only to reported data values, and query the author rather than rounding.

rules.quote: FAO uses the short scale for billions and trillions: 1 billion = one thousand million or 1 000 000 000 (10 9 ); 1 trillion = one million million or 1 000 000 000 000 (10 12 ).
rules.rule: Use the short scale: 1 billion = 10^9 (one thousand million); 1 trillion = 10^12 (one million million).

check.notes: Check that "billion"/"trillion" are used in the short-scale sense (e.g. in translated manuscripts where a long-scale billion = 10^12 may have been carried over). Conversion artefact: the exponents 10^9 and 10^12 appear as "10 / 9" and "10 / 12" on separate lines.

rules.quote_pdf: FAO uses the short scale for billions and trillions: {+1 billion }= one thousand million or 1 000 000 000 (10^9^); {+1 trillion }= one million million or 1 000 000 000 000 (10^12^).

rules.quote: Write fractions in words rather than numbers, using a hyphen, e.g. one-third.
rules.rule: Write fractions in words with a hyphen (one-third), not as numerals.

check.notes: Alternative 1: numeric fractions (1/3); crop years like 2015/16 and units like m/s are excluded. Alternative 2: unhyphenated fraction words ("one third"). "one fifth" etc. used as ordinal adjectives are rare false positives. Interaction with NUM-10-003 (numerals for measurements/percentages) is not addressed by the guide; prefer decimals there.

rules.quote_pdf: Write fractions in words rather than numbers, using a hyphen, e.g. {+one-third}.

rules.quote: Avoid the use of roman numerals except in established terminology, e.g. Type II error.
rules.rule: Avoid roman numerals except in established terminology.

check.notes: Flags roman numerals used as labels after common label words. Other roman numerals (e.g. list markers (i), (ii)) need agent review; lower-case roman numerals are permitted as source-note indicators in figures/tables/boxes (Table 11.1).

exceptions.quote: except in established terminology, e.g. Type II error.
exceptions.note: Established terminology keeps roman numerals.

rules.quote_pdf: Avoid the use of roman numerals except in established terminology, e.g. **{+Type II }**{+error}.

rules.quote: Where possible, write out ordinal numbers in full, e.g. the Thirteenth Session of the FAO Committee on Fisheries.
rules.rule: Where possible, write ordinal numbers out in full.

check.notes: Flags numeric ordinals (13th). Numerals are allowed "where it is necessary" (e.g. long ordinals), so Verify. Dates and centuries have their own rules (NUM-10_3-003, NUM-10_3-012).

correct: the Thirteenth Session of the FAO Committee on Fisheries

rules.quote_pdf: Where possible, write out ordinal numbers in full, e.g. {+the }**{+Thirteenth }**{+Session of the FAO Committee on Fisheries}.

correct: {+the }**{+Thirteenth }**{+Session of the FAO Committee on Fisheries}

ok: the Thirteenth Session of the FAO Committee on Fisheries

rules.quote: Where it is necessary to use numerals, do not use superscript for the ordinal indicator, e.g. the 13th Session, not the 13th Session.
rules.rule: When ordinals are written as numerals, do not superscript the ordinal indicator.

check.notes: Superscript cannot be seen in plain text or labelled markdown; check DOCX runs: a run with vertAlign=superscript containing st|nd|rd|th directly after a digit. Conversion artefact: the guide's own contrast example reads "the 13th Session, not the 13th Session" because the superscript was lost.

rules.quote_pdf: Where it is necessary to use numerals, do not use superscript for the ordinal indicator, e.g. {+the }**{+13th }**{+Session}, not {-the 13th Session}.

rules.quote: Avoid the use of adverbial ordinal numbers (firstly, secondly, thirdly, etc.), as subsequent numbers sound awkward. Replace these with first, second, third, etc.
rules.rule: Use first, second, third, etc. instead of firstly, secondly, thirdly, etc.

check.notes: Case-insensitive; keep initial capital when sentence-initial. Pairs beyond "thirdly" follow the guide's "etc.".

rules.quote_pdf: Avoid the use of adverbial ordinal numbers ({-firstly}, {-secondly}, {-thirdly}, etc.), as subsequent numbers sound awkward. Replace these with {+first}, {+second}, {+third}, etc.

rules.quote: For telephone numbers, be consistent in the use of parentheses and spaces.
rules.rule: Format telephone numbers consistently (parentheses and spaces).

check.notes: Collect telephone numbers and compare their parenthesis/space pattern.

rules.quote: Always include the country code using this format: (+39) or (+505).
rules.rule: Always include the country code in telephone numbers, in the form (+39).

check.notes: Flags a country code not enclosed in parentheses ("+39 06 ..."). Telephone numbers lacking any country code need agent review. False positives: signed values such as "+5%" or "UTC +6" written without parentheses.

rules.quote_pdf: Always include the country code using this format: {+(+39) }or {+(+505)}.

rules.quote: The recommended style is: (+39) 06 57057051.
rules.rule: Recommended telephone style: country code in parentheses, space, area code, space, number.

check.notes: Compare against the model (+39) 06 57057051.

rules.quote_pdf: The recommended style is: {+(+39) 06 57057051}.

rules.quote: To refer to a specific page: p. 40.
rules.rule: Refer to a single page as "p. 40" (p, full stop, space, number).

check.notes: Flags a missing space ("p.40") or missing full stop ("p 40"). False positive: statistical "p 0.05" written without an operator. Using "pp." for a single page needs agent review.

rules.quote_pdf: To refer to a specific page: {+p. 40.}

rules.quote: To refer to a page range: pp. 40–42.
rules.rule: Refer to a page range as "pp. 40–42" (pp., en dash between the numbers).

check.notes: Flags a hyphen in a page range, and "p." used with a range. Spaced en dashes ("pp. 40 – 42") are not flagged here.

rules.quote_pdf: To refer to a page range: {+pp. 40–42}.

rules.quote: To refer to the total number of pages in a publication: 120 pp.
rules.rule: Give the total number of pages of a publication as "120 pp.".

check.notes: Flags "120 p." and unspaced "120pp.". "8 p.m." is not matched. Applies mainly to reference lists.

rules.quote_pdf: To refer to the total number of pages in a publication: {+120 pp.}

rules.quote: Use the International System of Units (metric system) with equivalents in parentheses if necessary.
rules.rule: Use SI (metric) units; give other equivalents in parentheses only if necessary.

check.notes: Flags a quantity in a non-metric unit not directly inside an opening parenthesis. Equivalents in parentheses are permitted; shipping tons/cubic feet are an accepted exception (NUM-10_1-002). Verify, since conversion needs the author's data.

rules.quote: In general, use t onnes (equal to 1000 kg), not tons (2240 lb or approximately 1016 kg).
rules.rule: Use tonnes, not tons.

check.notes: Whole-word, case-insensitive. Skip shipping contexts (exception below). Conversion artefact: "tonnes" is split as "t / onnes" across lines 1513-1514.

exceptions.quote: For shipping, tons may however be appropriate. A shipping ton is used to measure the volume of freight, equivalent to 40 cubic feet (1.1 m 3 ) in the United States, or 42 cubic feet (1.2 m 3 ) in the United Kingdom.
exceptions.note: Shipping (freight volume) tons are acceptable.

rules.quote_pdf: In general, use {+tonnes }(equal to 1000 kg), not {-tons }(2240 lb or approximately 1016 kg).

rules.quote: A tonne is sometimes referred to in the United States as a metric ton, but always use the word tonne.
rules.rule: Write tonne, never metric ton.

check.notes: "metric tonne(s)" is included as a redundant variant of the prescribed word; drop those two pairs if a stricter reading is wanted.

rules.quote_pdf: A {+tonne }is sometimes referred to in the United States as a {-metric ton}, but always use the word {+tonne}.

rules.quote: A megatonne (Mt) is equivalent to one million tonnes.
rules.rule: Megatonne (Mt) = one million tonnes.

check.notes: Definition; supports checking that Mt is used for 10^6 tonnes.

rules.quote_pdf: A {+megatonne (Mt) }is equivalent to {+one million tonnes}.

rules.quote: Always give temperature in Celsius, not Fahrenheit, e.g. 35.5 °C.
rules.rule: Give temperatures in degrees Celsius, not Fahrenheit.

check.notes: Conversion needs the author's data; Verify.

rules.quote_pdf: Always give temperature in Celsius, not Fahrenheit, e.g. {+35.5 °C}.

rules.quote: TABLE 10.1 _ Common units Unit Symbol metre m square metre m 2 cubic metre m 3 micron μ litre l,L gram g tonne t second s degree Celsius °C degree absolute K Kilocalorie kcal hour h
rules.rule: Use the unit symbols in Table 10.1: m, m2, m3, μ (micron), l or L, g, t, s, °C, K, kcal, h.

check.notes: The table gives correct symbols only, no incorrect forms, so no wordlist is built. Symbol lists in NUM-10_1-007..012 draw on it. Conversion artefacts: superscript 2/3 of m2/m3 on separate lines; "Kilocalorie" capitalized (cell start). The guide lists "μ" for micron as written. Litre may be l or L; the guide does not say whether one must be used consistently.

rules.quote: Do not use punctuation or letter spacing in such units as cm, mm, g, °C.
rules.rule: Do not put full stops in, or space out the letters of, unit symbols.

check.notes: Flags dotted symbols (c.m., "5 cm. of"), "° C" and letter-spaced symbols. A unit followed by a full stop is flagged only when the next word is lower case (i.e. not the sentence end).

rules.quote_pdf: Do not use punctuation or letter spacing in such units as {+cm}, {+mm}, {+g}, {+°C}.

rules.quote: Note, however, that there should always be a non-breaking space between the number and the unit, e.g. 3 cm, 70 g, 37 °C.
rules.rule: Always put a non-breaking space between a number and its unit symbol.

check.notes: Flags a missing space ("3cm", "37°C"). "s" (second) is omitted to avoid matching decades (1990s). Ordinary vs non-breaking space can only be distinguished on raw DOCX text (U+00A0/U+202F); markdown exports normalize it. Does not apply to % (NUM-10_2-004) or to degrees of latitude/longitude (10°30').

rules.quote_pdf: Note, however, that there should always be a non-breaking space between the number and the unit, e.g. {+3 cm}, {+70 g}, {+37 °C.}

rules.quote: Do not use the plural for abbreviations of units (e.g. 7 kg, not 7 kgs).
rules.rule: Do not add a plural s to unit abbreviations.

check.notes: Only symbols from Table 10.1 and the guide's text are included.

rules.quote_pdf: Do not use the plural for abbreviations of units (e.g. {+7 }**{+kg}**{+, }not {-7 kgs}).

rules.quote: To indicate per, use /, as in 3 m/s (rather than 3 m s -1 ).
rules.rule: Indicate "per" with a slash (3 m/s), not a negative exponent.

check.notes: In plain text the superscript -1 appears inline ("m s-1", "m s -1"). Conversion artefact: double space in "in  3 m/s" and the exponent on a separate line.

rules.quote_pdf: To indicate {-per}, use {+/}, as in {+3 }**{+m/s }**(rather than {-3 m s}^{--1}^).

rules.quote: Avoid combinations of three units such as: Production is 25 tonnes/ha/year. Prefer: Annual production is 25 tonnes/ha. Exceptions may be made for statistical documents.
rules.rule: Avoid combining three units (25 tonnes/ha/year); rephrase (Annual production is 25 tonnes/ha).

check.notes: Requires a number before the unit chain to avoid URLs and and/or constructions. Statistical documents are exempt. Note the guide uses the word "tonnes" with the symbol "ha" in its own example.

exceptions.quote: Exceptions may be made for statistical documents.
exceptions.note: Statistical documents.

rules.quote_pdf: Avoid combinations of three units such as: {-Production is 25 tonnes/ha/year}. Prefer: **{+Annual }**{+production is }**{+25 tonnes/ha}**. Exceptions may be made for statistical documents.

rules.quote: In series of measurements, use the symbol each time: 10 cm, 20 cm and 50 cm, not 10, 20 and 50 cm.
rules.rule: Repeat the unit symbol after every value in a series of measurements.

check.notes: Flags a comma-separated series of bare numbers ending with a single unit. Two-item ranges ("from 10 to 20 cm") are not covered by the guide and are not flagged.

rules.quote_pdf: In series of measurements, use the symbol each time: {+10 }**{+cm}**{+, 20 }**{+cm }**{+and 50 }**{+cm}**, not {-10, 20 and 50 cm}.

rules.quote: Correct ways of writing latitude and longitude include: 10°30' north; 90° west; the zone from 10° to 40° north.
rules.rule: Write latitude and longitude as in the models: 10°30' north; 90° west; from 10° to 40° north (direction as a word).

rules.quote_pdf: Correct ways of writing latitude and longitude include: {+10°30' north}; {+90° west}; {+the zone from 10° to 40° north}.

rules.quote: Use the abbreviations N, E, S and W only in tables.
rules.rule: Use the compass abbreviations N, E, S and W only in tables; write the words in text.

check.notes: Flags a coordinate followed by N/E/S/W outside tables. Do not run on table scope.

rules.quote_pdf: Use the abbreviations {+N}, {+E}, {+S }and {+W }only in tables.

rules.quote: For minutes and seconds of latitude or longitude (41°16'40" south) a straight apostrophe or straight quotation mark may be used rather than the prime symbol (‘).
rules.rule: For minutes and seconds of latitude/longitude, straight apostrophe and straight quotation mark are acceptable instead of prime symbols.

check.notes: Permissive: do not flag straight ' or " in coordinates. Conversion artefact: the prime symbol is rendered as a left single quotation mark (U+2018) in the file; a checker must not treat curly quotes as the prescribed alternative. Curly quotes in coordinates are not addressed by the guide.

rules.quote_pdf: For minutes and seconds of latitude or longitude ({+41°16'40" south}) a straight apostrophe or straight quotation mark may be used rather than the prime symbol ({-‘}).

rules.quote: If your reader may not immediately understand the unit abbreviation, include it in the list of abbreviations or spell out the full name once: 100 hectares (ha).
rules.rule: Introduce an unfamiliar unit abbreviation in the list of abbreviations or by spelling it out once with the symbol in parentheses.

check.notes: Treat unit symbols beyond the very common ones as abbreviations needing first-use definition or a list entry; which units the reader "may not immediately understand" is a judgement (Verify).

rules.quote_pdf: If your reader may not immediately understand the unit abbreviation, include it in the list of abbreviations or spell out the full name once: {+100 hectares (ha)}.

rules.quote: Use percent (never per cent)
rules.rule: Write percent, never per cent.

check.notes: Case-insensitive. "per-cent" is a typographic variant of the forbidden form.

rules.quote_pdf: Use {+percent }(never {-per cent})

rules.quote: rather than the symbol % in text, e.g. Exports increased by 16 percent in the last quarter.
rules.rule: In running text, write percent rather than the % symbol.

check.notes: Do not run on table/figure scope, where % is required (NUM-10_2-003). Captions and notes to tables/figures: the guide does not say; Verify.

rules.quote_pdf: rather than the symbol {-% }in text, e.g. {+Exports increased by 16 }**{+percent }**{+in the last quarter.}

rules.quote: In tables and figures, use the symbol
rules.rule: In tables and figures, use the % symbol rather than the word percent.

check.notes: Run on table cells and figure text only. Column headings such as "Share (percent)" are not addressed by the guide; Verify.

rules.quote: with no space between the number and the symbol, e.g. 16%.
rules.rule: In tables and figures, put no space between the number and %.

check.notes: Includes ordinary and non-breaking spaces.

rules.quote_pdf: with no space between the number and the symbol, e.g. {+16%}.

rules.quote: Write dates in this order: Monday, 16 October 2000
rules.rule: Write dates as (weekday,) day month year.

rules.quote_pdf: Write dates in this order: {+Monday, 16 October 2000}

rules.quote: (with no comma between the date and the month, or the month and the year)
rules.rule: Put no comma between day and month or between month and year.

rules.quote: Do not use ordinal numbers for dates (e.g. 1 January, not 1st January).
rules.rule: Do not use ordinal numbers in dates.
rules.quote_pdf: Do not use ordinal numbers for dates (e.g. {+1 January}, not {-1st January}).

rules.quote: Avoid starting a sentence with a year, but if it is unavoidable it must be written out: Nineteen ninety-eight was not a leap year.
rules.rule: Avoid starting a sentence with a year; if unavoidable, write the year out in words.

correct: Nineteen ninety-eight was not a leap year.

rules.rule: Do not abbreviate years.

rules.quote_pdf: Do not abbreviate years, e.g. {+1985}, not {-’85}.

rules.quote: Decades are referred to in complete numerals (e.g. the 1990s; not the nineties, the ’90s or the 90s).
rules.rule: Write decades in complete numerals (the 1990s).

rules.quote_pdf: Decades are referred to in complete numerals (e.g. {+the 1990s}; not t{-he nineties}, {-the ’90s }or {-the 90s}).

rules.quote: When indicating a range of values or dates, there are two possible forms: - from ... to or between ... and, e.g. from 1970 to 1987; or - with an en-dash, e.g. The 1970–1987 period was ...
rules.rule: Express a range of values or dates with from ... to, between ... and, or an en dash.

rules.quote_pdf: Do not combine the two forms, e.g. {-from 1970–1987}.

rules.quote_pdf: Note that for a crop or fiscal year, exceptionally, an abbreviated version should be used ({+2015/16}, not {-2015/2016}).

rules.rule: Write centuries out in full.
rules.quote_pdf: Centuries should be written out in full, e.g. {+the twenty-first century}, not {-the 21st century.}

rules.rule: Prefer the 24-hour clock.

rules.quote_pdf: The use of the 24-hour system is preferred, e.g. {+08.00}, {+13.30.}

rules.quote: For works with more than ten authors, only the first seven must be listed; the rest may optionally be truncated using et al.
rules.rule: In reference entries, et al. may replace authors only beyond the first seven, and only for works with more than ten authors.

check.notes: Flags et al. after fewer than seven listed authors (e.g. "Smith, J., Brown, K. et al. 2010.") and "Sanders et al. 2011." as a list entry. An entry with 7+ named authors then et al. but fewer than 11 authors in reality needs the source (Author). Implicit: works with up to ten authors list all authors (not stated in words).

Sanders, J., Cohen, L. & Bolbol, M. 2010.

rules.quote_pdf: For works with more than ten authors, only the first seven must be listed; the rest may optionally be truncated using {+et al.}

rules.quote: Use and or the ampersand (&) between the names of the last two authors in each reference, e.g.: Sanders, J., Cohen, L. & Bolbol, M. 2010.
rules.rule: In reference entries, join the last two authors with "and" or "&".

check.notes: Flags author lists where the last two names are joined by a comma only ("Sanders, J., Cohen, L., Bolbol, M. 2010."). Contrast in-text rule REF-12_3_1-003 (no &). The guide does not require consistency between "and" and "&" across entries; all Table 12.1 samples use "&".

rules.quote: Titles of books, journals, papers, periodicals and websites are italicized, including titles in foreign languages. Titles of articles, presentations and chapters are not italicized, including titles in foreign languages.
rules.rule: Italicize titles of books, journals, papers, periodicals and websites; do not italicize titles of articles, presentations and chapters.

check.notes: Needs formatting runs (DOCX) or markdown emphasis. Classify entry type (journal article: article title roman, journal name italic; book/report: title italic; chapter: chapter title roman, book title italic). Box 12.3 adds: database names may be italic if consistent (REF-12_8_1-017).

rules.quote: Titles of FAO information products use sentence case, whereas meetings, official days and years, projects and conferences are given initial capitalization.
rules.rule: In references, titles of FAO products are in sentence case; names of meetings, official days/years, projects and conferences take initial capitals.

check.notes: Agent flags FAO-authored entries whose titles are in title case. check.notes: Needs formatting runs. Flag bold on titles, years or publishers; bold author names are optional and should then be consistent.

rules.section_title: WRITING OR GENERATING BIBLIOGRAPHIC LISTS (Box 12.1 Best practices for non-English sources)
rules.quote: When the language of the publication and the language of a source are not the same, updating the source to a corresponding full version in the language of the publication is the best possible solution.
rules.rule: Where a source exists in full in the publication language, cite that version.

rules.section_title: WRITING OR GENERATING BIBLIOGRAPHIC LISTS (Box 12.1 Best practices for non-English sources)
rules.quote: If only a translated summary is available, cite the full original source and add the title of the summary (in parentheses) following the title.
rules.rule: If only a translated summary exists, cite the original and add the summary title in parentheses after the title.

rules.section_title: WRITING OR GENERATING BIBLIOGRAPHIC LISTS (Box 12.1 Best practices for non-English sources)
rules.quote: If no official translation exists, provide a translated title [in square brackets] following the original language title
rules.rule: For non-English titles without an official translation, add a translated title in square brackets after the original title.

check.notes: Agent/language detection: a non-English title not followed by a bracketed English title. The translation itself may need the author.
